setup_steps.title: Install a code editor
setup_steps.body: Download Visual Studio Code and run the installer. It's free, and it colors your code so mistakes are easier to spot.

setup_steps.title: Make your first page
setup_steps.body: Make a new folder called my-site and open it in your editor. Add a file called index.html and type your name in it. Save the file.

setup_steps.title: Open it in a browser
setup_steps.body: Double-click index.html in your file explorer. Your browser opens it and you see your name. After each change, save the file and refresh the browser.

project_ideas.title: A page for your org
project_ideas.brief: Build one web page that introduces an org or club you care about. Say what it does, show a photo, list upcoming events, and add a form for people who want to join.
done_when: The page opens in a browser without anything missing.
It has a heading, a paragraph, an image and a link.
It has a list or a table of events.
It has a form with at least two labeled fields.

topics.title: Page structure
topics.summary: Write the basic skeleton that every web page is built on.
topics.why_it_matters: A browser needs to know what your page contains and how it's organized. HTML is how you tell it.

key_terms.definition:
A word in angle brackets, like

, that marks a part of a page.
An opening tag, a closing tag and everything between them.

topics.explanation:
A text file on its own is just text. To show a heading, a picture or a link, the browser needs labels that say what each part is. Those labels are called tags. Most tags come in pairs. An opening tag like

starts something, and a closing tag like

ends it. Together with the content inside, they make an element. Every page has the same skeleton. says this is a modern web page. The element wraps everything. Inside it, holds information about the page, such as its title. holds everything people actually see.
topics.example: Hello!

Close every tag you open. A missing

Save the file and refresh the browser after each change, or you'll keep seeing the old page.

topics.title: Text and headings
topics.summary: Organize a page's text with headings, paragraphs and emphasis.
topics.why_it_matters: A wall of text is hard to read. Headings and paragraphs let people, search engines and screen readers find what they need.

key_terms.definition: A title for a section of the page, from <h1> down to <h6>.
Chosen for what the content means, not how it looks.

topics.explanation:
Browsers ignore the line breaks and extra spaces in your file. If you want separate paragraphs, you have to mark them with

. Headings go from

to

. Use

once for the main title of the page,

for sections, and

for parts of a section. Pick a level for its place in the outline, not for its size. You'll change how it looks later with CSS. For emphasis inside a sentence, use for something important and for stress. Screen readers can use these tags, so they carry meaning that plain bold or italic text doesn't.
topics.example:
Coding Club

What we do

We meet every Friday to build small projects.

Beginners are very welcome.
tips: Don't skip levels. Go from <h2> to <h3>, not straight from <h2> to <h5>.

Pressing Enter in your file doesn't start a new paragraph on the page. Use a new

.

topics.title: Links and images
topics.summary: Connect pages with links and add images that everyone can understand.
topics.why_it_matters: Links are what make the web a web, and images make a page worth looking at. Both need a few details to work properly.

key_terms.definition: Extra information in an opening tag, like href="page.html".
A description of an image for people who can't see it.

topics.explanation: Some tags need more information to do their job. A link needs to know where it goes, and an image needs to know which file to show. You give that information with attributes, written inside the opening tag as name="value". A link uses the tag. Its href attribute holds the address, and the text between the tags is what people click. An image uses the tag, which has no closing tag. Its src attribute says which file to show. Its alt attribute describes the image. Screen readers read the alt text aloud, and it also appears if the image fails to load.
topics.example: Visit our school
tips: If an image doesn't show, check the file name, including capital letters, and that the file is in the folder you think it is.
Write link text that makes sense alone. "See our events" is better than "click here".

skill_questions.prompt: Which attribute sets where a link goes?

choices: Describing the image for people who can't see it
Adding a caption under the image

topics.title: Lists and tables
topics.summary: Show groups of items in lists and data in tables.
topics.why_it_matters: Steps, menus and schedules are easier to read when they're laid out clearly. Lists and tables give that kind of content a proper structure.

key_terms.definition: One horizontal line of cells in a table, written with <tr>.

topics.explanation:
Use a list when you have several items of the same kind. <ul> makes an unordered list with bullets. <ol> makes an ordered list with numbers, for steps or rankings. Either way, each item goes inside its own <li>.

Use a table when your data has rows and columns, like a schedule. <table> wraps everything and <tr> makes each row. Inside a row, <th> is a heading cell and <td> is a normal data cell.

Notice the nesting: items sit inside lists, and cells sit inside rows. Indenting your code to match makes it much easier to spot mistakes. Tables are for data only, not for arranging a page.
topics.example:
1. Register
  2. Join the group chat
DayEvent
FridayWorkshop
tips: Only <li> can go directly inside <ul> or <ol>. Plain text there is a mistake.
Every row of a table should have the same number of cells, or the columns won't line up.

topics.title: Forms
topics.summary: Build a form that collects information from visitors.
topics.why_it_matters: Sign-ups, surveys and search boxes all need a way for visitors to type something in. Forms are how a page listens.

key_terms.definition: A group of fields that visitors fill in and send.
The text that says what a field is for.

topics.explanation:
So far your pages only talk. A form lets visitors talk back. The
element wraps all the fields. The tag makes most fields, and its type attribute decides which kind: text, email, checkbox and more. Like , it has no closing tag. A
topics.example:
<form>
  <label for="email">Your email</label> <!-- for matches the id -->
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Join</button>
</form>
tips: A label's for must match the input's id exactly, or they won't be connected.
Use type="email" for email addresses. The browser checks the format, and phones show a better keyboard.
